questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Periodic motion: time period, frequency, displacement as a function of time
questions.question: A simple pendulum completes 40 oscillations in 20 s. What is the frequency of its oscillation?

solution.key_concept: The time period is the time for one oscillation, and $\nu = 1/T$.
steps: Time period $T = 20/40 = 0.5$ s.
Frequency $\nu = 1/T = 1/0.5 = 2$ Hz.
solution.why_not_others: 0.5 Hz is the value of T in seconds, not the frequency. $4\pi$ is the angular frequency in rad/s, wrongly given in Hz. 40 Hz takes the total oscillation count as the frequency.
solution.common_trap: Writing the time period, or the angular frequency $\omega = 2\pi\nu$, as the frequency.
solution.time_saving_tip: Frequency = number of oscillations ÷ time taken = 40/20.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Periodic motion: time period, frequency, displacement as a function of time
questions.question: Which of the following motions is periodic but NOT oscillatory?
options: A simple pendulum swinging with small amplitude
A particle moving in uniform circular motion
A block oscillating at the end of a horizontal spring
The prong of a vibrating tuning fork

solution.key_concept: Oscillatory motion is periodic to-and-fro motion about a mean position. Not every periodic motion is oscillatory.
steps: Uniform circular motion repeats after a fixed time, so it is periodic.
It is not a to-and-fro motion about a mean position, so it is not oscillatory.
The pendulum, the spring-block and the tuning-fork prong all move to and fro about a mean position.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): A particle moving in uniform circular motion
solution.why_not_others: Each of the other three moves to and fro about an equilibrium position, so each is both periodic and oscillatory.
solution.common_trap: Assuming every periodic motion must also be oscillatory.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Periodic motion: time period, frequency, displacement as a function of time
questions.question: A particle oscillates with an angular frequency of $10\pi\ \text{rad s}^{-1}$. How many complete oscillations does it make in 3 s?

solution.key_concept: $\omega = 2\pi\nu$, so $\nu = \omega/2\pi$.
steps: Number of oscillations in 3 s $= 5 \times 3 = 15$.
solution.why_not_others: 30 comes from taking $\nu = \omega/\pi$. 94 treats $\omega$ itself as the frequency ($10\pi \times 3 \approx 94$). 7.5 comes from dividing by $4\pi$.
solution.common_trap: Treating angular frequency in rad/s as frequency in Hz.
solution.time_saving_tip: Divide $\omega$ by $2\pi$ first; the $\pi$ cancels at once.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Periodic motion: time period, frequency, displacement as a function of time
questions.question: Given below are two statements: Assertion A and Reason R. Choose the correct answer.

statements.R: Oscillatory motion is a to-and-fro motion about a mean position that repeats itself after equal intervals of time.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

solution.key_concept: Oscillatory motion is defined as periodic motion about a mean position.
steps: By definition, an oscillation repeats after equal time intervals, so it is periodic. A is true.
R states this definition correctly, so R is true.
Because the definition itself contains the repetition, R directly explains A.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
solution.why_not_others: Both statements are true, so options 3 and 4 fail. R is the very reason A holds, so option 2 fails.
solution.common_trap: Mixing up the direction of the relationship: the converse (every periodic motion is oscillatory) is false.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Periodic motion: time period, frequency, displacement as a function of time
questions.question: Given below are two statements. Choose the most appropriate answer.

statements.I: In an oscillating system, the quantity called 'displacement' need not be a linear distance; it may be an angle, a pressure change or an electric field.
statements.II: A body that makes 50 oscillations per second has a time period of 0.02 s and an angular frequency of $50\ \text{rad s}^{-1}$.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

solution.key_concept: Displacement is a general variable whose nature depends on the system. Also, $\omega = 2\pi\nu$.
steps: Statement I: displacement can be linear, angular, a pressure change or an electric field. It is correct.
Statement II: $T = 1/50 = 0.02$ s is correct.
However, $\omega = 2\pi \times 50 = 100\pi \approx 314\ \text{rad s}^{-1}$, not 50. So Statement II is incorrect.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
solution.why_not_others: Statement II has a correct period but a wrong angular frequency, so any option calling it correct fails. Statement I is fully correct, so options 2 and 4 fail.
solution.common_trap: Accepting Statement II after checking only its first part (the period).
solution.time_saving_tip: Check every number in a compound statement.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Periodic functions
questions.question: Which of the following functions of time is non-periodic?

solution.key_concept: A function is periodic if $f(t+T) = f(t)$. Exponential functions never repeat.
steps: $e^{-\omega t}$ decreases steadily and never takes the same value again, so it is non-periodic.
The other three are sinusoids or sums of sinusoids, so all are periodic.
solution.why_not_others: $\sin\omega t+\cos\omega t$ has period $2\pi/\omega$. $\sin^2\omega t$ has period $\pi/\omega$. $\sin\omega t+\sin2\omega t$ is periodic, although it is not SHM.
solution.common_trap: Thinking that a sum of sinusoids with different $\omega$ is non-periodic. It is periodic but not simple harmonic.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Periodic functions
questions.question: The displacement of a particle is $x = 3\sin(100t) + 4\cos(100t)$, where x is in cm and t in s. What is the amplitude of its motion?

solution.key_concept: $a\sin\omega t + b\cos\omega t$ is SHM with amplitude $\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$.
steps: Here $a = 3$ and $b = 4$.
Amplitude $= \sqrt{9+16} = 5$ cm.
solution.why_not_others: 7 cm adds the coefficients directly. 1 cm subtracts them. $\sqrt{7}$ cm wrongly takes the square root of their sum.
solution.common_trap: Adding the coefficients as if the two terms were in phase.
solution.time_saving_tip: Recognise the 3-4-5 triple.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Periodic functions
questions.question: The function $y = \sin^2(\pi t)$, where t is in seconds, is periodic. What is its period?

solution.key_concept: $\sin^2\omega t = (1-\cos2\omega t)/2$ has period $\pi/\omega$.
steps: Here $\omega = \pi$ rad/s.
Period $= \pi/\omega = \pi/\pi = 1$ s.
solution.why_not_others: 2 s is the period of $\sin\pi t$ itself. 0.5 s halves the period twice. 4 s doubles it instead of halving it.
solution.common_trap: Using $2\pi/\omega$ for a squared sinusoid.
solution.time_saving_tip: Squaring a sinusoid doubles its angular frequency, so the period is halved.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Periodic functions
questions.question: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct answer.

list_I.label: A
list_I.text: $\sin\omega t + \cos\omega t$

list_I.label: B
list_I.text: $\sin^2\omega t$

list_I.label: C
list_I.text: $\sin\omega t + \sin2\omega t$

list_I.label: D
list_I.text: $e^{-\omega t}$

list_II.label: III
list_II.text: SHM about mean value 1/2 with period $\pi/\omega$

solution.key_concept: Classify each function: combinations of the same $\omega$ give SHM, squared sinusoids give SHM at $2\omega$, mixed $\omega$ gives periodic non-SHM, and exponentials are non-periodic.
steps: A: $\sin\omega t + \cos\omega t = \sqrt{2}\sin(\omega t+\pi/4)$, which is SHM with period $2\pi/\omega$. So A-II.
B: $\sin^2\omega t = (1-\cos2\omega t)/2$, which is SHM about 1/2 with period $\pi/\omega$. So B-III.
C: the two terms have different angular frequencies, so it is periodic but not SHM. So C-IV.
D: the exponential is non-periodic. So D-I.
solution.why_not_others: Option 2 calls $\sin^2\omega t$ non-SHM and the mixed sum SHM. Option 3 swaps the periods of A and B. Option 4 wrongly calls the mixed-frequency sum SHM.
solution.common_trap: Treating $\sin^2\omega t$ as non-SHM, or treating any sum of sinusoids as SHM.
solution.time_saving_tip: D-I is common to all options, so focus on A, B and C.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Periodic functions
questions.question: Which of the following statements about periodic functions are correct?

statements.B: $\sin\omega t + \sin2\omega t$ represents simple harmonic motion.
statements.C: $a\sin\omega t + b\cos\omega t$ represents SHM with amplitude $\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$.
statements.D: $\log\omega t$ is a periodic function of time.
statements.E: Any periodic function can be expressed as a superposition of sines and cosines of different time periods with suitable coefficients.

solution.key_concept: Periodicity, the SHM condition, and the superposition of sinusoids.
steps: A is true: $\cos^2\omega t = (1+\cos2\omega t)/2$, so its period is $\pi/\omega$.
B is false: the terms have different $\omega$, so the sum is periodic but not SHM.
C is true: the two terms combine into a single sinusoid of amplitude $\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$.
D is false: the logarithm is non-periodic.
E is true: this is the stated superposition property of periodic functions.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): A, C and E only
solution.why_not_others: Option 2 includes B, which is false. Option 3 includes D, which is false. Option 4 leaves out E, which is true.
solution.common_trap: Taking 'periodic' to mean 'simple harmonic'.
solution.time_saving_tip: Once B and D are ruled out, only options 1 and 4 remain; checking E settles it.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Simple harmonic motion, its equation and phase
questions.question: A particle executes SHM with amplitude 0.05 m and angular frequency $20\ \text{rad s}^{-1}$. What is its maximum speed?

solution.key_concept: $v_{max} = A\omega$, reached at the mean position.
solution.why_not_others: 20 is $A\omega^2$, the maximum acceleration. 0.0025 is $A/\omega$. 2 uses $2A\omega$, wrongly taking the peak-to-peak distance as the amplitude.
solution.common_trap: Mixing up the formulas for maximum speed and maximum acceleration.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Simple harmonic motion, its equation and phase
questions.question: A particle executes SHM with amplitude 10 cm and angular frequency $4\ \text{rad s}^{-1}$. What is its speed when its displacement from the mean position is 6 cm?

solution.key_concept: $v = \omega\sqrt{A^2 - x^2}$
steps: $v = 4 \times 8 = 32\ \text{cm s}^{-1}$.
solution.why_not_others: 24 uses $\omega x$. 40 is the maximum speed $A\omega$. 16 uses $\omega(A - x)$.
solution.common_trap: Subtracting the displacements directly instead of their squares.
solution.time_saving_tip: 6-8-10 is a Pythagorean triple.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Simple harmonic motion, its equation and phase
questions.question: In simple harmonic motion, by what phase angle does the acceleration of the particle lead its velocity?

solution.key_concept: Velocity leads displacement by $\pi/2$, and acceleration leads displacement by $\pi$.
steps: Phase of velocity relative to displacement = $+\pi/2$.
Phase of acceleration relative to displacement = $+\pi$.
So acceleration leads velocity by $\pi - \pi/2 = \pi/2$.
solution.why_not_others: $\pi$ is the lead of acceleration over displacement, not over velocity. Zero and $\pi/4$ have no basis in the SHM phase relations.
solution.common_trap: Answering with the acceleration-displacement phase difference.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Simple harmonic motion, its equation and phase
questions.question: Given below are two statements: Assertion A and Reason R. Choose the correct answer.

statements.A: In SHM, the speed of the particle is maximum at the extreme positions.
statements.R: In SHM, the magnitude of acceleration is maximum at the extreme positions.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

solution.key_concept: In SHM, speed is maximum at the mean position and zero at the extremes, while acceleration is maximum at the extremes.
steps: Speed $\omega\sqrt{A^2-x^2}$ is zero at $x = \pm A$, so A is false.
Acceleration $|a| = \omega^2|x|$ is maximum ($A\omega^2$) at $x = \pm A$, so R is true.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): A is false but R is true
solution.why_not_others: A is false, so options 1, 2 and 3 all fail.
solution.common_trap: Assuming that maximum acceleration means maximum speed.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Simple harmonic motion, its equation and phase
questions.question: Given below are two statements. Choose the most appropriate answer.

statements.I: A particle executing SHM with a time period of 2.4 s takes 0.2 s to move from the mean position to a point midway between the mean position and an extreme position.
statements.II: The graph of acceleration versus displacement for a particle in SHM is a straight line with a positive slope of $\omega^2$.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

solution.key_concept: The time from the mean position to $A/2$ is $T/12$. Also, $a = -\omega^2 x$.
steps: Statement I: $T/12 = 2.4/12 = 0.2$ s, so it is correct.
Statement II: since $a = -\omega^2 x$, the slope is $-\omega^2$, which is negative. So it is incorrect.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
solution.why_not_others: Statement II has the wrong sign of slope. Statement I is numerically correct, so options 2 and 4 fail.
solution.common_trap: Using T/6 or T/8 for the mean-to-A/2 interval, or ignoring the minus sign in $a = -\omega^2 x$.
solution.time_saving_tip: Remember: mean to A/2 takes T/12, and A/2 to the extreme takes T/6.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Oscillations of a spring: restoring force and force constant
questions.question: A block of mass 0.5 kg is attached to an ideal spring of force constant $50\ \text{N m}^{-1}$ on a smooth horizontal surface. What is the time period of its oscillations?

solution.key_concept: $T = 2\pi\sqrt{m/k}$
steps: $T = 2\pi \times 0.1 = 0.2\pi = \pi/5$ s.
solution.why_not_others: $20\pi$ s uses $\sqrt{k/m}$, i.e. the ratio inverted. 0.1 s leaves out the $2\pi$. $\pi/10$ s uses $\pi$ instead of $2\pi$.
solution.common_trap: Inverting the ratio of m and k.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Oscillations of a spring: restoring force and force constant
questions.question: A spring-mass system has a time period T on the Earth. It is taken to the Moon, where the acceleration due to gravity is one-sixth of that on the Earth. What is its time period on the Moon?

solution.key_concept: The period of a spring-mass system depends only on m and k: $T = 2\pi\sqrt{m/k}$.
steps: Neither m nor k changes on the Moon.
So the period stays T.
solution.why_not_others: $T\sqrt{6}$ is what a simple pendulum would show. $T/\sqrt{6}$ and $6T$ wrongly bring g into the formula.
solution.common_trap: Applying the pendulum's dependence on g to a spring-mass system.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Oscillations of a spring: restoring force and force constant
questions.question: A spring of force constant $60\ \text{N m}^{-1}$ is cut into three equal parts. Two of these parts are connected in parallel. What is the effective force constant of the combination?

solution.key_concept: Since $k \propto 1/l$, each of n equal parts has constant nk. In parallel, the constants add.
steps: Each part has $k = 3 \times 60 = 180\ \text{N m}^{-1}$.
In parallel: $180 + 180 = 360\ \text{N m}^{-1}$.
solution.why_not_others: 40 takes each part as $k/3$. 90 combines the parts in series. 120 ignores the effect of cutting.
solution.common_trap: Thinking a shorter piece of spring is softer.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Oscillations of a spring: restoring force and force constant
questions.question: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct answer.

list_I.label: A
list_I.text: Mass m on a single spring of constant k

list_I.label: B
list_I.text: Mass hanging from a vertical spring with static extension $\Delta l$

list_I.label: C
list_I.text: Mass m on springs $k_1$ and $k_2$ in series

list_I.label: D
list_I.text: Mass m on springs $k_1$ and $k_2$ in parallel

solution.key_concept: Use $T = 2\pi\sqrt{m/k_{eff}}$ with the correct effective constant for each arrangement.
steps: A: $T = 2\pi\sqrt{m/k}$, so A-II.
B: $k\Delta l = mg$, so $m/k = \Delta l/g$ and A-IV... that is, B-IV.
C: $k_{series} = k_1k_2/(k_1+k_2)$, so C-III.
D: $k_{parallel} = k_1+k_2$, so D-I.
solution.why_not_others: Option 2 swaps the series and parallel formulas. Option 3 swaps A and B. Option 4 mismatches B and C.
solution.common_trap: Swapping the series and parallel effective constants.
solution.time_saving_tip: Series is softer, so it gives the longer period (the larger expression).

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Oscillations of a spring: restoring force and force constant
questions.question: Which of the following statements about spring and spring-like oscillators are correct?

statements.A: The time period of a spring-mass system is independent of its amplitude.
statements.B: For a mass on a vertical spring, gravity changes the time period because it changes the equilibrium extension.
statements.C: When a spring of constant k is cut into n equal parts, each part has a force constant k/n.
statements.D: For a floating cylinder oscillating vertically, the time period is inversely proportional to the square root of the liquid's density.
statements.E: Two springs connected in series behave as a softer spring than either one alone.

solution.key_concept: Spring-mass period, spring combinations, and the general rule $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\text{inertia}/\text{restoring force per unit displacement}}$.
steps: A is true: $T = 2\pi\sqrt{m/k}$ contains no amplitude.
B is false: gravity only shifts the mean position; T is unchanged.
C is false: each part has constant nk, since $k \propto 1/l$.
D is true: $T = 2\pi\sqrt{L\rho_c/(\rho_l g)}$, so $T \propto 1/\sqrt{\rho_l}$.
E is true: $k_{series} = k_1k_2/(k_1+k_2)$ is smaller than both $k_1$ and $k_2$.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): A, D and E only
solution.why_not_others: Option 1 leaves out E. Option 2 includes B, which is false. Option 3 includes B and C and leaves out A and D.
solution.common_trap: Believing that cutting a spring makes each piece softer, or that gravity alters the period of a vertical spring.
solution.time_saving_tip: Ruling out B and C leaves only options 1 and 4; check E to decide.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Energy in SHM: kinetic and potential energies
questions.question: A particle executes simple harmonic motion of amplitude $A$. When its displacement from the mean position is $A/2$, what fraction of its total mechanical energy is kinetic?

solution.key_concept: In SHM, $U = \frac{1}{2}kx^2$ and $K = \frac{1}{2}k(A^2 - x^2)$, with total energy $E = \frac{1}{2}kA^2$.
steps: So $K = E - U = \frac{3E}{4}$.
The fraction of energy that is kinetic is $\frac{3}{4}$.
solution.why_not_others: $\frac{1}{4}$ is the potential-energy fraction. $\frac{1}{2}$ holds only at $x = A/\sqrt{2}$. $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ is the ratio of the speed to the maximum speed, not an energy ratio.
solution.common_trap: Swapping the K and U fractions, or using a velocity ratio in place of an energy ratio.
solution.time_saving_tip: Remember: at $x = A/2$, $U = E/4$ and $K = 3E/4$.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Energy in SHM: kinetic and potential energies
questions.question: A block of mass 0.5 kg attached to a spring of force constant 200 N/m oscillates on a smooth horizontal surface with amplitude 0.1 m. What is its kinetic energy when its displacement is 0.06 m?

steps: Check: $U = 0.36$ J and $E = 1.00$ J, so $K + U = E$.
solution.why_not_others: 0.36 J is the potential energy at this position. 0.16 J comes from wrongly using $(A - x)^2$ instead of $A^2 - x^2$. 1.00 J is the total energy.
solution.common_trap: Using $(A - x)^2$ in place of $(A^2 - x^2)$.
solution.time_saving_tip: Find E and U first, then take $K = E - U$.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Energy in SHM: kinetic and potential energies
questions.question: The displacement of a particle executing SHM is $x = 0.05\sin(10\pi t)$ m, with t in seconds. What is the frequency with which its kinetic energy varies?

solution.key_concept: Kinetic and potential energies in SHM oscillate at twice the frequency of the motion.
steps: $\omega = 10\pi$ rad/s, so $\nu = \omega/2\pi = 5$ Hz.
The kinetic energy varies with frequency $2\nu = 10$ Hz.
solution.why_not_others: 5 Hz is the frequency of the displacement, not of the energy. 2.5 Hz wrongly halves it. 20 Hz comes from doubling twice.
solution.common_trap: Taking the frequency of the energy oscillation as $\nu$ instead of $2\nu$.
solution.time_saving_tip: Since $K \propto \cos^2\omega t$, the energy frequency is $2\nu$.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Energy in SHM: kinetic and potential energies
questions.question: Given below are two statements: Assertion A and Reason R. Choose the correct answer.

statements.A: The kinetic energy of a particle executing SHM of time period T varies periodically with period T.
statements.R: The kinetic energy of a particle in SHM is maximum at the mean position, and the particle passes through the mean position twice in every cycle.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

solution.key_concept: Kinetic energy in SHM varies with period T/2.
steps: K is maximum each time the particle crosses the mean position.
This happens twice per cycle, so K repeats every T/2.
So A is false and R is true.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): A is false but R is true
solution.why_not_others: A is false, so any option that calls A true is ruled out.
solution.common_trap: Assuming that energies share the period of the displacement.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Energy in SHM: kinetic and potential energies
questions.question: Given below are two statements. Choose the most appropriate answer.

statements.I: For a given mass executing SHM, if the frequency is doubled while the amplitude is kept the same, the total mechanical energy becomes four times its original value.
statements.II: For a spring-mass oscillator, the graph of speed v against displacement x is an ellipse, which becomes a circle only when the spring constant k (in N/m) and the mass m (in kg) are numerically equal.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

solution.key_concept: $E = \frac{1}{2}m\omega^2A^2$, and the energy relation gives an ellipse in the x-v plane.
steps: $E \propto \omega^2$ at fixed m and A, so doubling the frequency multiplies E by 4. Statement I is correct.
From $\frac{1}{2}mv^2 + \frac{1}{2}kx^2 = E$: $\frac{v^2}{\omega^2A^2} + \frac{x^2}{A^2} = 1$, which is an ellipse.
It is a circle when $\omega = 1$, that is, when k = m numerically. Statement II is correct.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
solution.why_not_others: Both statements follow directly from the energy relations, so no option rejecting either one is valid.
solution.common_trap: Thinking that energy depends only on amplitude, or picking $k = 1/m$ as the circle condition.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Simple pendulum and its time period
questions.question: A simple pendulum of length 1 m has a time period of 2 s at a place. What is the time period of a simple pendulum of length 4 m at the same place, for small oscillations?

solution.key_concept: $T \propto \sqrt{l}$
solution.why_not_others: 8 s assumes $T \propto l$. $2\sqrt{2}$ s takes the square root of the wrong factor. 1 s inverts the relation.
solution.common_trap: Assuming the period is proportional to the length.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Simple pendulum and its time period
questions.question: A simple pendulum has a time period of 2 s when at rest. It is placed in a lift accelerating upward at $g/3$. What is its new time period? (Take $\sqrt{3} = 1.73$.)

solution.key_concept: In a lift accelerating upward, $g_{eff} = g + a$.
steps: $T' = T\sqrt{g/g_{eff}} = 2\sqrt{3/4} = \sqrt{3} = 1.73$ s.
solution.why_not_others: 2.31 s comes from inverting the ratio. 1.50 s takes T proportional to $1/g$ instead of $1/\sqrt{g}$. 2.00 s ignores the acceleration of the lift.
solution.common_trap: Using $g - a$ for upward acceleration, or forgetting the square root.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Simple pendulum and its time period
questions.question: Due to a rise in temperature, the length of the pendulum of a clock increases by 0.2%. The clock was correct before the change. What happens to the clock in one day (86400 s)?

solution.key_concept: $\frac{\Delta T}{T} = \frac{1}{2}\frac{\Delta l}{l}$
steps: A longer period means the clock runs slow, so it loses time.
Time lost per day $= 0.001 \times 86400 = 86.4$ s.
solution.why_not_others: 'Gains' has the wrong direction. 172.8 s omits the factor $\frac{1}{2}$. 43.2 s applies the factor $\frac{1}{2}$ twice.
solution.common_trap: Forgetting the factor 1/2, or concluding that the clock gains time.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Simple pendulum and its time period
questions.question: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct answer.

list_I.label: A
list_I.text: Pendulum in a lift accelerating upward with acceleration a

list_I.label: B
list_I.text: Pendulum in a lift accelerating downward with acceleration a (a < g)

list_I.label: C
list_I.text: Pendulum in a freely falling lift

list_I.label: D
list_I.text: Pendulum in a car accelerating horizontally with acceleration a

solution.key_concept: Replace g by $g_{eff}$ in accelerating frames.
steps: Upward acceleration: $g_{eff} = g + a$, so A matches IV.
Downward acceleration: $g_{eff} = g - a$, so B matches I.
Free fall: $g_{eff} = 0$, so there is no oscillation and C matches II.
Horizontal acceleration: $g_{eff} = \sqrt{g^2 + a^2}$, so D matches III.
solution.why_not_others: Option (2) swaps the upward and downward cases. Option (3) swaps the free-fall and horizontal cases. Option (4) assigns the horizontal formula to the upward lift.
solution.common_trap: Mixing up the signs for upward and downward acceleration.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Simple pendulum and its time period
questions.question: Which of the following statements about a simple pendulum are correct?

statements.A: Its time period is independent of the mass of the bob.
statements.B: Its effective length is measured from the point of suspension to the top of the bob.
statements.C: A girl who stands up on a swing decreases its time period.
statements.D: Its time period on the Moon is smaller than on the Earth.
statements.E: The relation $T = 2\pi\sqrt{l/g}$ is valid only for small angular amplitudes.

options: A, C, D and E only

solution.key_concept: $T = 2\pi\sqrt{l/g}$ holds for small angles, with l measured to the centre of the bob.
steps: A is true: T does not depend on the mass of the bob.
B is false: l is measured to the centre of the bob.
C is true: standing up raises the centre of mass, so l and T decrease.
D is false: g is smaller on the Moon, so T is larger.
E is true: the formula relies on $\sin\theta \approx \theta$.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): A, C and E only
solution.why_not_others: Option (1) omits E. Option (2) includes the false B. Option (3) includes the false D.
solution.common_trap: Measuring l to the top of the bob, or thinking T decreases on the Moon.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Wave motion: longitudinal and transverse waves
questions.question: Which of the following cannot propagate through the bulk of air?
options: Waves consisting of compressions and rarefactions

solution.key_concept: Transverse mechanical waves need shear rigidity, which fluids lack.
steps: Air has no shear rigidity, so transverse mechanical waves cannot travel through its bulk.
Longitudinal waves (compressions and rarefactions) and EM waves can travel through air.
solution.why_not_others: Sound in air is longitudinal, and option (4) describes the same type of wave. EM waves need no medium at all.
solution.common_trap: Thinking that EM waves, being transverse, cannot pass through air.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Wave motion: longitudinal and transverse waves
questions.question: Which of the following can be exhibited by transverse waves but never by longitudinal waves?

solution.key_concept: Polarisation is possible only for transverse waves.
steps: All waves transport energy and momentum.
Longitudinal waves also travel through solids.
Only transverse waves can be polarised.
solution.why_not_others: Energy transfer, momentum transfer and propagation through solids are shared by both wave types.
solution.common_trap: Thinking that longitudinal waves cannot travel in solids.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Wave motion: longitudinal and transverse waves
questions.question: Ripples on the surface of water are best described as:
options: A combination of transverse and longitudinal waves

solution.key_concept: In surface ripples, water particles move both perpendicular to and along the direction of propagation.
steps: Surface water waves combine transverse and longitudinal motion.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): A combination of transverse and longitudinal waves
solution.why_not_others: The visible crests suggest purely transverse waves, but the particles also move along the direction of propagation. The waves are not purely longitudinal, and they are mechanical, not electromagnetic.
solution.common_trap: Calling ripples purely transverse because crests and troughs are visible.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Wave motion: longitudinal and transverse waves
questions.question: Given below are two statements: Assertion A and Reason R. Choose the correct answer.

statements.A: Sound cannot travel through vacuum, whereas light can.
statements.R: Sound waves are transverse, while light waves are longitudinal.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

solution.key_concept: Sound is a mechanical wave that needs a medium; light is an EM wave that needs none.
steps: A is true: sound needs a medium, while light does not.
R is false: sound in air is longitudinal, and light (EM) is transverse.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): A is true but R is false
solution.why_not_others: R reverses the nature of the two waves, so any option calling R true is wrong.
solution.common_trap: Linking the need for a medium to the wave being transverse or longitudinal rather than mechanical or EM.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Wave motion: longitudinal and transverse waves
questions.question: Given below are two statements. Choose the most appropriate answer.

statements.I: Transverse mechanical waves can travel through the bulk of a liquid because a liquid possesses inertia.
statements.II: The propagation of a mechanical wave requires the medium to possess both elasticity and inertia.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

solution.key_concept: Transverse mechanical waves need shear rigidity; every mechanical wave needs elasticity and inertia.
steps: A liquid lacks shear rigidity, so transverse waves cannot travel through its bulk. Statement I is incorrect.
Mechanical waves need both elasticity and inertia. Statement II is correct.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
solution.why_not_others: Inertia alone cannot support a transverse wave without shear rigidity, so Statement I is false. Statement II is correct.
solution.common_trap: Assuming any material medium can carry transverse waves.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Speed of a travelling wave
questions.question: A sound wave of frequency 500 Hz has a wavelength of 0.68 m in air. What is the speed of sound in air?

solution.key_concept: $v = \nu\lambda$
solution.why_not_others: 735 m/s comes from $\nu/\lambda$. $1.36 \times 10^{-3}$ m/s comes from $\lambda/\nu$. 680 m/s doubles the correct value.
solution.common_trap: Dividing instead of multiplying.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Speed of a travelling wave
questions.question: A string of mass 5 g and length 50 cm is stretched with a tension of 36 N. What is the speed of transverse waves on the string?

solution.key_concept: $v = \sqrt{T/\mu}$, with $\mu$ in kg/m.
solution.why_not_others: 600 m/s comes from keeping the length in cm ($\mu = 10^{-4}$). 3600 m/s omits the square root. 1.9 m/s comes from keeping the mass in grams ($\mu = 10$).
solution.common_trap: Mixing units when computing $\mu$.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Speed of a travelling wave
questions.question: The speed of sound in a gas at $27^\circ C$ is v. At what temperature will the speed become 2v, with the pressure kept constant?

solution.key_concept: $v \propto \sqrt{T}$, where T is absolute temperature.
steps: Doubling v requires $T' = 4T = 4 \times 300 = 1200$ K.
solution.why_not_others: $108^\circ C$ multiplies the Celsius temperature by 4. $1200^\circ C$ forgets to convert back from kelvin. $54^\circ C$ assumes $v \propto T$ and uses the Celsius scale.
solution.common_trap: Using Celsius temperature in $v \propto \sqrt{T}$.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Speed of a travelling wave
questions.question: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct answer.

list_I.label: A
list_I.text: Pressure of a gas doubled at constant temperature

list_I.label: B
list_I.text: Absolute temperature of a gas made four times

list_I.label: C
list_I.text: Mass per unit length of a string made four times at the same tension

list_I.label: D
list_I.text: Tension in a string made nine times

solution.key_concept: In a gas, $v = \sqrt{\gamma P/\rho} \propto \sqrt{T}$. On a string, $v = \sqrt{T/\mu}$.
steps: At constant temperature, $P/\rho$ is constant, so v is unchanged: A matches II.
$v \propto \sqrt{T}$, so a fourfold temperature doubles v: B matches IV.
$v \propto 1/\sqrt{\mu}$, so a fourfold $\mu$ halves v: C matches I.
$v \propto \sqrt{T}$ (tension), so a ninefold tension triples v: D matches III.
solution.why_not_others: Option (1) wrongly lets pressure change v. Option (2) inverts the string relations. Option (3) inverts the temperature dependence and the $\mu$ dependence.
solution.common_trap: Believing that pressure changes the speed of sound.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Speed of a travelling wave
questions.question: Which of the following statements about the speed of waves are correct?

statements.A: Newton assumed isothermal compressions in sound and obtained about 280 m/s for air.
statements.B: Laplace treated the compressions as adiabatic, giving $v = \sqrt{\gamma P/\rho}$.
statements.C: Sound travels slower in moist air than in dry air because moist air is denser.
statements.D: When a wave passes into another medium, its frequency changes while its wavelength stays the same.
statements.E: In general, the speed of sound is greatest in solids and least in gases.

solution.key_concept: Laplace correction, effect of humidity, and invariance of frequency across media.
steps: A and B are true statements of the Newton and Laplace treatments.
C is false: moist air is less dense, so sound travels faster in it.
D is false: frequency stays the same, while speed and wavelength change.
E is true: $v_{solid} > v_{liquid} > v_{gas}$.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): A, B and E only
solution.why_not_others: Options (1) and (4) include the false C. Option (3) includes the false D and omits A.
solution.common_trap: Thinking moist air is denser, or that frequency changes between media.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Displacement relation for a progressive wave
questions.question: A transverse wave on a string is described by $y = 0.05\sin(4\pi x - 200\pi t)$, where x and y are in metres and t is in seconds. What are the speed and direction of propagation of the wave?

solution.key_concept: Wave speed $v = \omega/k$. The form $(kx-\omega t)$ means the wave travels along +x.
steps: Here $k = 4\pi$ rad/m and $\omega = 200\pi$ rad/s.
$v = \omega/k = 200\pi/4\pi = 50$ m/s.
x and t have opposite signs, so the wave moves along +x.
solution.why_not_others: Option (1) has the wrong direction. Option (3) is $k/\omega$, which is inverted. Option (4) is $a\omega$, the maximum particle speed, not the wave speed.
solution.common_trap: Confusing the maximum particle speed $a\omega$ with the wave speed $\omega/k$.
solution.time_saving_tip: Wave speed = coefficient of t divided by coefficient of x.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Displacement relation for a progressive wave
questions.question: A sound wave of frequency 500 Hz travels with a speed of 360 m/s. What is the phase difference between two points on its path that are 0.12 m apart?

solution.key_concept: Phase difference $\Delta\phi = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda}\Delta x$.
steps: $\Delta\phi = \frac{2\pi}{0.72}\times 0.12 = \frac{2\pi}{6} = \pi/3$.
solution.why_not_others: $\pi/6$ comes from dropping the factor 2 in $2\pi$. $2\pi/3$ comes from doubling the path difference. $\pi/2$ would need a separation of $\lambda/4 = 0.18$ m.
solution.common_trap: Forgetting to find $\lambda$ first, or using $\pi/\lambda$ in place of $2\pi/\lambda$.
solution.time_saving_tip: Since $0.12/0.72 = 1/6$ of a wavelength, the phase difference is $2\pi/6$.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Displacement relation for a progressive wave
questions.question: For a progressive wave $y = 0.004\sin(50x - 400t)$ (SI units), what is the ratio of the maximum particle speed to the wave speed?

solution.key_concept: $v_{p,max} = a\omega$ and $v = \omega/k$, so $v_{p,max}/v = ak$.
steps: $v_{p,max} = a\omega = 0.004 \times 400 = 1.6$ m/s.
solution.why_not_others: 5 is the inverse ratio. 1 assumes the particle speed equals the wave speed. 0.4 uses the peak-to-peak value 2a in place of a.
solution.common_trap: Treating particle velocity and wave velocity as the same quantity.
solution.time_saving_tip: Directly use $v_{p,max}/v = ak$.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Displacement relation for a progressive wave
questions.question: Given below are two statements: Assertion A and Reason R. Choose the correct answer.

statements.A: For a progressive wave $y = a\sin(kx-\omega t)$, the maximum speed of a particle of the medium is equal to the wave speed $\omega/k$.
statements.R: In a progressive wave, the particle velocity equals $-v\,\partial y/\partial x$, where v is the wave speed.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

solution.key_concept: Maximum particle speed is $a\omega$, while wave speed is $\omega/k$. They are linked by $v_p = -v\,\partial y/\partial x$.
steps: Maximum particle speed $= a\omega$, which in general is not $\omega/k$. So A is false.
$\partial y/\partial t = -a\omega\cos(kx-\omega t)$ and $\partial y/\partial x = ak\cos(kx-\omega t)$, so $v_p = -(\omega/k)\,\partial y/\partial x$. So R is true.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): A is false but R is true
solution.why_not_others: A is false, so options (1), (2) and (3) are ruled out.
solution.common_trap: Equating particle speed with wave speed. Their ratio is $ak$, the maximum slope of the wave.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Displacement relation for a progressive wave
questions.question: Given below are two statements. Choose the most appropriate answer.

statements.I: If both the amplitude and the frequency of a progressive wave are doubled, its intensity becomes four times.
statements.II: The wave $y = 0.01\sin(2\pi x + 600\pi t)$ (SI units) travels along the negative x-direction with a speed of 300 m/s.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

solution.key_concept: $I \propto a^2\omega^2$. The form $(kx+\omega t)$ means the wave travels along -x, and $v = \omega/k$.
steps: Doubling a and $\omega$ multiplies I by $2^2\times 2^2 = 16$, not 4. So I is incorrect.
x and t have the same sign, so the wave moves along -x.
$v = 600\pi/2\pi = 300$ m/s. So II is correct.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
solution.why_not_others: Statement I ignores the $\omega^2$ dependence of intensity. Statement II is fully consistent with the notes.
solution.common_trap: Remembering only $I \propto a^2$ and forgetting the $\omega^2$ factor.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Principle of superposition and reflection of waves
questions.question: Two waves of the same frequency, with amplitudes 3 mm and 4 mm, superpose at a point with a phase difference of $\pi/2$. What is the amplitude of the resultant wave?

solution.why_not_others: 7 mm is the constructive value ($\phi = 0$). 1 mm is the destructive value ($\phi = \pi$). 3.5 mm is just the average of the two amplitudes.
solution.common_trap: Adding the amplitudes directly regardless of the phase difference.
solution.time_saving_tip: At $\phi = \pi/2$ the amplitudes add like perpendicular vectors.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Principle of superposition and reflection of waves
questions.question: Two coherent waves with intensities in the ratio 9 : 1 interfere. What is the ratio of the maximum to the minimum intensity in the interference pattern?

solution.key_concept: $I_{max}/I_{min} = \left(\frac{a_1+a_2}{a_1-a_2}\right)^2$, with $I \propto a^2$.
steps: Amplitude ratio $a_1 : a_2 = \sqrt{9} : \sqrt{1} = 3 : 1$.
solution.why_not_others: 9 is just the given intensity ratio. 2 comes from forgetting to square. $25/16$ comes from putting intensities into the formula in place of amplitudes.
solution.common_trap: Using intensities directly in the amplitude formula.
solution.time_saving_tip: Always convert intensities to amplitudes by taking square roots first.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Principle of superposition and reflection of waves
questions.question: An incident wave $y_i = a\sin(kx - \omega t)$ is reflected from a rigid boundary at x = 0, and the reflected wave is $y_r = a\sin(kx + \omega t)$. Which of the following is correct?
options: The reflected wave has angular frequency $2\omega$
The reflected wave travels along the positive x-direction
The point x = 0 is an antinode of the resulting wave
The resultant is $2a\sin kx\cos\omega t$, with a node at x = 0

solution.key_concept: Reflection at a rigid end gives a node at the boundary. Frequency does not change on reflection.
steps: $\sin(kx-\omega t)+\sin(kx+\omega t) = 2\sin kx\cos\omega t$.
At x = 0, $\sin kx = 0$, so the displacement is always zero there: x = 0 is a node.
The reflected wave has the same $\omega$, and $(kx+\omega t)$ means it moves along -x.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): The resultant is $2a\sin kx\cos\omega t$, with a node at x = 0
solution.why_not_others: Frequency never changes on reflection. The reflected wave travels along -x. A rigid end is a node, not an antinode.
solution.common_trap: Thinking reflection changes frequency, or placing an antinode at a fixed end.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Principle of superposition and reflection of waves
questions.question: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct answer.

list_I.label: A
list_I.text: Two waves, each of amplitude a, superposed with phase difference 0

list_I.label: B
list_I.text: Two waves, each of amplitude a, superposed with phase difference $\pi$

list_I.label: C
list_I.text: Two waves, each of amplitude a, superposed with phase difference $\pi/2$

list_I.label: D
list_I.text: Two waves, each of amplitude a, superposed with phase difference $2\pi/3$

solution.key_concept: $A = \sqrt{2a^2(1+\cos\phi)}$ for two equal amplitudes.
steps: $\phi = \pi/2$: $A = \sqrt{2}a$.
$\phi = 2\pi/3$: $\cos\phi = -1/2$, so $A = \sqrt{a^2} = a$.
solution.why_not_others: The other matchings swap the $\pi/2$ and $2\pi/3$ results, or swap the constructive and destructive cases.
solution.common_trap: Taking $\cos(2\pi/3)$ as +1/2.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Principle of superposition and reflection of waves
questions.question: Which of the following statements about superposition and reflection of waves are correct?

statements.A: A wave reflected from a rigid boundary suffers a phase change of $\pi$.
statements.B: A pulse reflected from a free end is inverted.
statements.C: The frequency of a wave does not change on reflection.
statements.D: After two waves overlap, each continues to travel unaffected.
statements.E: For destructive interference of waves with amplitudes $a_1$ and $a_2$, the resultant amplitude is $a_1 + a_2$.

options: A, C, D and E only

solution.key_concept: Rigid end: phase change $\pi$. Free end: no phase change. Frequency is unchanged on reflection. Superposed waves pass through each other unaltered.
steps: A is true: a rigid boundary gives a phase change of $\pi$.
B is false: a free end gives no phase change, so the pulse is not inverted.
C and D are true, as stated in the principle of superposition and the rules of reflection.
E is false: destructive interference gives $|a_1 - a_2|$.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): A, C and D only
solution.why_not_others: Every other option includes B or E, both of which are false.
solution.common_trap: Mixing up the free-end and rigid-end behaviour.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Standing waves in strings and organ pipes; fundamental mode and harmonics
questions.question: A string 0.5 m long is fixed at both ends. Transverse waves travel on it at 200 m/s. What is its fundamental frequency?

solution.key_concept: For a string fixed at both ends, $\nu_1 = v/2L$.
solution.why_not_others: 100 Hz uses the closed-pipe formula $v/4L$. 400 Hz uses $v/L$. 50 Hz uses $v/8L$.
solution.common_trap: Using the closed-pipe formula for a string.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Standing waves in strings and organ pipes; fundamental mode and harmonics
questions.question: A pipe 0.85 m long is closed at one end. The speed of sound is 340 m/s; neglect end correction. What is the frequency of its second overtone?

solution.key_concept: A closed pipe has only odd harmonics, so its second overtone is the 5th harmonic.
steps: Fundamental $= v/4L = 340/3.4 = 100$ Hz.
The overtones are the 3rd and 5th harmonics, so the second overtone $= 5\times 100 = 500$ Hz.
solution.why_not_others: 300 Hz is the first overtone. 200 Hz is the fundamental of an open pipe of the same length. 400 Hz assumes even harmonics are present.
solution.common_trap: Taking the second overtone as the 3rd harmonic.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Standing waves in strings and organ pipes; fundamental mode and harmonics
questions.question: A string 1.2 m long, fixed at both ends, vibrates at 250 Hz in a standing wave pattern with 4 antinodes. What is the speed of transverse waves on the string?

solution.key_concept: In the nth harmonic, a string fixed at both ends has n antinodes and $L = n\lambda/2$.
steps: 4 antinodes means n = 4.
$v = \nu\lambda = 250\times 0.6 = 150$ m/s.
solution.why_not_others: 300 m/s takes $\lambda = 1.2$ m. 200 m/s treats the 4 as nodes, giving n = 3. 75 m/s takes each antinode as spanning only $\lambda/4$.
solution.common_trap: Confusing the count of nodes with the count of antinodes.
solution.time_saving_tip: The number of loops equals the number of antinodes, and each loop is $\lambda/2$ long.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Standing waves in strings and organ pipes; fundamental mode and harmonics
questions.question: Given below are two statements: Assertion A and Reason R. Choose the correct answer.

statements.A: The fundamental frequency of a pipe closed at one end is half that of an open pipe of the same length.
statements.R: In a standing sound wave, pressure nodes are located at displacement antinodes.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

solution.key_concept: Closed pipe: $\nu_1 = v/4L$. Open pipe: $\nu_1 = v/2L$.
steps: $v/4L$ is half of $v/2L$, so A is true.
R is a true statement about where pressure and displacement nodes lie.
A follows from the closed end being a node and the open end an antinode (L = $\lambda/4$), not from the pressure–displacement relation.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
solution.why_not_others: Both statements are true, so options (3) and (4) are out. R does not explain why the closed pipe's fundamental is halved, so option (1) is out.
solution.common_trap: Picking option (1) simply because both statements are true.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Standing waves in strings and organ pipes; fundamental mode and harmonics
questions.question: Given below are two statements. Choose the most appropriate answer.

statements.I: A pipe closed at one end, vibrating in its 7th harmonic, has 4 displacement nodes, counting the closed end.
statements.II: A standing wave transports energy from one end of the medium to the other at the wave speed.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

solution.key_concept: In the pth harmonic, a closed pipe has $(p+1)/2$ nodes. A standing wave transports no net energy.
steps: Nodes $= (7+1)/2 = 4$, so I is correct.
A standing wave transports no net energy, so II is incorrect.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
solution.why_not_others: Statement II contradicts the basic property of standing waves, and Statement I is correct.
solution.common_trap: Counting 7 nodes for the 7th harmonic, or forgetting to count the closed end.
solution.time_saving_tip: Sketch the pattern: the closed end is N and the open end is A, with $\lambda/4$ segments in between.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Beats
questions.question: Two tuning forks of frequencies 256 Hz and 260 Hz are sounded together. How many beats are heard per second?

solution.key_concept: Beat frequency $= |\nu_1 - \nu_2|$.
steps: $|260 - 256| = 4$ beats per second.
solution.why_not_others: 2 is half the difference. 258 Hz is the frequency of the tone heard. 516 is the sum of the frequencies.
solution.common_trap: Confusing the beat frequency with the average tone frequency.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Beats
questions.question: An unknown tuning fork produces 6 beats per second with a standard fork of 384 Hz. When the unknown fork is loaded with a little wax, the number of beats per second decreases. What was the original frequency of the unknown fork?

solution.key_concept: Wax lowers frequency. If the beats then decrease, the unknown fork was the higher-frequency one.
steps: Possible frequencies: $384 \pm 6$, that is 390 Hz or 378 Hz.
Lowering the frequency reduces the beat count only if the unknown fork was above 384 Hz.
So the unknown frequency is 390 Hz.
solution.why_not_others: With 378 Hz, wax would increase the beats. 384 Hz would give no beats. 396 Hz uses twice the beat count.
solution.common_trap: Getting the wax logic backwards.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Beats
questions.question: Two sources of frequencies 498 Hz and 504 Hz are sounded together. What is the time interval between two successive maxima of loudness?

solution.key_concept: Beat period $= 1/|\nu_1 - \nu_2|$.
steps: Beat frequency $= 504 - 498 = 6$ Hz.
Beat period $= 1/6$ s.
solution.why_not_others: $1/12$ s halves the period. $1/3$ s is the period of the envelope factor $\cos(\pi\Delta\nu t)$, which has two loudness maxima per cycle. $1/501$ s is the period of the tone heard.
solution.common_trap: Taking the period of $\cos(\pi\Delta\nu t)$ as the beat period.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Beats
questions.question: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct answer.

list_I.label: A
list_I.text: Number of beats per second for frequencies $\nu_1$ and $\nu_2$

list_I.label: B
list_I.text: Frequency of the tone actually heard

list_I.label: C
list_I.text: Loading a tuning fork with wax

list_I.label: D
list_I.text: Filing the prongs of a tuning fork

solution.key_concept:
Beat frequency is $|
u_1-
u_2|$ and the tone heard is $
u_{av}$. Wax lowers a fork's frequency; filing raises it.
steps: A matches II and B matches III.
C matches IV (wax lowers frequency) and D matches I (filing raises frequency).
solution.why_not_others: The other options swap the beat and average frequencies, or reverse the wax and file effects.
solution.common_trap: Reversing the effects of wax and filing.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Beats
questions.question: Which of the following statements about beats are correct?

statements.A: The ear can distinguish beats only when the frequency difference is about 10 Hz or less.
statements.B: Sources of 300 Hz and 306 Hz together produce a tone of 303 Hz whose loudness rises and falls 6 times per second.
statements.C: If loading the unknown fork with wax increases the beat count, the unknown fork had the higher frequency.
statements.E: Filing the prongs of a tuning fork lowers its frequency.

options: A, B, C and D only

solution.key_concept:
Beat frequency is $|
u_1-
u_2|$ and the tone heard is $
u_{av}$. Wax lowers frequency; filing raises it.
steps: A is true: beats are audible only up to about 10 per second.
B is true: $\nu_{av} = 303$ Hz and the beat frequency is 6 Hz.
C is false: an increase in beats means the unknown fork had the lower frequency.
D is true. E is false, because filing raises the frequency.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): A, B and D only
solution.why_not_others: Option (1) misses the true statement B. Options (3) and (4) include the false statements C or E.
solution.common_trap: Inverting the wax-test conclusion.
